issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The Maladaptive Strategies node mixes avoidance behaviours with what appears to be a trigger-like cue. 'Seeing people that I socialised with before the event' is phrased as a social reminder/trigger rather than a coping strategy, so within the specified node it is clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts' and 'Avoid Intimacy' imply social withdrawal, which can fit PTSD, but the specific target 'seeing people that I socialised with before the event' suggests avoidance of trauma reminders tied to the past. This sits awkwardly with the selected Negative Appraisals, which focus on incapacity, moral injury, and not belonging, without any corresponding interpersonal mistrust, shame in relationships, or reminder-based social threat theme.

issues.item: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere' is possible in PTSD, but here it leans toward a broad identity/interpersonal alienation theme that is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The Threat items are predominantly hypervigilant safety-checking and pursuit fears, while the other appraisal items emphasize incapacity and violated values; this makes the belonging item feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent appraisal cluster.

vignette: Kaito's life changed forever on a sweltering summer evening three years ago. He was working late at the bank in downtown Manhattan when a terrorist attack shook the city. Gunfire erupted outside, and Kaito watched in horror as people ran for cover, screaming and bleeding. The sounds of shattering glass and crumbling concrete still echoed in his mind. In the chaos, he had managed to hide under his desk, but the feeling of powerlessness lingered. In the aftermath, Kaito became withdrawn, avoiding social gatherings and intimate relationships. He told himself it was because he didn't want to burden others with his problems, but deep down, he feared getting close to people would make him vulnerable again. His divorce from his high school sweetheart a year after the attack seemed like a natural consequence of this emotional numbing. They had grown apart, and Kaito couldn't shake off the feeling that he was no longer capable of being the partner she needed. As time passed, Kaito found solace in overwork. He would often volunteer for extra shifts or take on additional responsibilities to avoid being alone with his thoughts. His colleagues praised his dedication, but they began to notice a change in him – the irritability, the short fuse that would ignite at the slightest provocation. One day, he lashed out at a customer who had asked him a simple question, reducing the poor woman to tears. The incident left Kaito shaken, and he started wondering if he was losing control. At night, Kaito's sleep was fitful, punctuated by waking moments when he would sit up with a start, his heart racing, as he checked whether he was safe. He would get out of bed to scan the room, ensuring that no one was lurking in the shadows. This behavior had become so ingrained that even during the day, he found himself frequently looking behind him, checking if someone was following him. Kaito's self-perception had taken a hit as well. He felt like he had acted against his own values by hiding under the desk instead of trying to help others during the attack. The guilt still lingered, and he couldn't shake off the feeling that he wasn't trustworthy. When confronted with difficult decisions at work or in his personal life, Kaito would second-guess himself, wondering if he was truly capable of making sound judgments. Despite his best efforts to suppress thoughts about the trauma, fragments of that day continued to seep into his consciousness. He would see a news report about terrorism, and suddenly he was back under the desk, reliving the horror. The memories were no longer just painful reminders; they had become a threat, a constant reminder of his own vulnerability. Kaito's relationships with his family and friends began to fray as well. They expressed concern about his behavior, but he pushed them away, convinced that he was beyond help. His job performance started to suffer too, as the irritability and lack of focus took their toll. It was then that Kaito realized he needed professional help. With a sense of trepidation, Kaito scheduled an appointment with a therapist, hoping to finally confront the demons that had haunted him for so long. As he sat in the waiting room, flipping through a worn copy of People magazine, he couldn't shake off the feeling that he was taking a step into the unknown – and that it might just be his only chance at redemption.
